AP Macroeconomics.learning_target_s:
CH 1 [CED 1.1, 1.2]
EQ: Why does scarcity force every person and society to make trade-offs? (1.1) • What does a choice really cost, and how do rational people use marginal thinking and incentives? (1.1, 1.2)
CH 2 [CED 1.1, 1.2; 2.1 preview]
EQ: How do economists use models like the PPC to show scarcity, opportunity cost, and growth? (1.2) • How do economists separate what is from what ought to be? (1.1)
CH 3 [CED 1.3]
EQ: Why do people and countries specialize and trade, even when one side is better at producing everything? (1.3)
AP Macroeconomics.success_criteria:
I can define scarcity and explain why it requires choices. (1.1)
I can identify the opportunity cost of a decision, including explicit and implicit costs. (1.2)
I can apply marginal analysis and explain how incentives change behavior. (1.1)
I can describe how market and command systems answer the basic economic questions. (1.1)
I can draw a PPC and identify efficient, inefficient, and unattainable points. (1.2)
I can calculate constant and increasing opportunity cost from a PPC and explain what its shape means. (1.2)
I can show economic growth or contraction as a shift of the PPC. (1.2)
I can distinguish positive from normative statements and explain ceteris paribus. (1.1)
I can describe the circular-flow model. (2.1 preview)
I can determine absolute and comparative advantage from output or input data. (1.3)
I can calculate opportunity cost and identify the range of mutually beneficial terms of trade. (1.3)
I can show on a PPC how specialization and trade let a country consume beyond its PPC. (1.3)

AP Macroeconomics.unit: UNIT 5 — Fiscal & Monetary Policy, Inflation–Unemployment Trade-off, Deficits & Debt
AP Macroeconomics.learning_target_s:
CH 34 [CED 3.8, 3.9, 3.2, 5.1, 5.4, 5.5]
EQ: How can government spending and taxes close an output gap, and what limits their effectiveness? (3.8, 3.9) • How do fiscal and monetary policy work together in the short run? (5.1) • When do deficits and debt crowd out private investment and growth? (5.4, 5.5)
CH 35 [CED 5.2, 5.1]
EQ: Is there a trade-off between inflation and unemployment, and why does it disappear in the long run? (5.2) • How do expectations and supply shocks shift the Phillips curve? (5.2)
AP Macroeconomics.success_criteria:
I can identify the expansionary or contractionary fiscal policy for a gap and calculate the required change in G or T using multipliers. (3.8, 3.2)
I can explain automatic stabilizers and how they differ from discretionary policy. (3.9)
I can show the combined effects of fiscal and monetary actions on AD–AS, the money market, and loanable funds. (5.1)
I can distinguish a budget deficit from the national debt and explain how one changes the other. (5.4)
I can show crowding out on the loanable funds graph and explain its effect on long-run growth. (5.5)
I can explain policy lags and other limits of stabilization policy. (3.8, 5.1)
I can graph the short-run and long-run Phillips curves and link points on them to AD–AS. (5.2)
I can show a movement along the SRPC caused by an AD shift. (5.2)
I can show a shift of the SRPC caused by a change in inflation expectations or a supply shock. (5.2)
I can explain stagflation and the costs of reducing inflation. (5.1, 5.2)

AP Microeconomics.learning_target_s:
CH 1 [CED 1.1, 1.2, 1.5, 1.6]
EQ: Why does scarcity force every person, firm, and society to make trade-offs? (1.1) • How do rational people use marginal thinking and incentives to make decisions? (1.5, 1.6)
CH 2 [CED 1.2, 1.3] — class time on PPF & circular flow only; rest via summer reading
EQ: How do economists use models like the PPF to show scarcity, opportunity cost, and growth? (1.3) • What is the difference between a positive and a normative statement? (1.2)
CH 3 [CED 1.4]
EQ: Why do people and countries specialize and trade, even when one side is better at producing everything? (1.4)
AP Microeconomics.success_criteria:
I can define scarcity and explain why it requires choices and opportunity costs. (1.1)
I can explain how markets and government each allocate resources and why markets usually do it well. (1.2)
I can apply marginal analysis and cost–benefit reasoning to a decision and explain how incentives change behavior. (1.5, 1.6)
I can draw a PPF and identify efficient, inefficient, and unattainable points. (1.3)
I can calculate constant and increasing opportunity cost from a PPF and explain what its shape means. (1.3)
I can show growth or a change in resources/technology as a shift of the PPF. (1.3)
I can distinguish positive from normative statements and describe the circular-flow model. (1.2)
I can determine absolute and comparative advantage from output or input data. (1.4)
I can calculate opportunity cost and identify the range of mutually beneficial terms of trade. (1.4)
I can show on a PPF how specialization and trade let a country consume beyond its PPF. (1.4)

AP Microeconomics.learning_target_s:
CH 4 [CED 2.1, 2.2, 2.6, 2.7]
EQ: What determines how much of a good buyers want and sellers offer at each price? (2.1, 2.2) • How does a competitive market reach equilibrium, and what happens when demand or supply shifts? (2.6, 2.7)
CH 5 [CED 2.3, 2.4, 2.5]
EQ: Why do buyers and sellers respond more strongly to a price change for some goods than others? (2.3, 2.5) • How can a seller know whether raising price will raise or lower total revenue? (2.3) • How do economists use elasticity to tell whether goods are related, or a necessity vs. a luxury? (2.4) • Why can good news for an industry (a bumper crop) be bad news for its producers? (2.3, 2.6)
CH 6 [CED 2.8]
EQ: When the government sets a price or imposes a tax, who really wins, who really loses, and why? (2.8)
AP Microeconomics.success_criteria:
I can explain the laws of demand and supply and distinguish movement along a curve from a shift. (2.1, 2.2)
I can identify the determinants of demand and supply and predict the direction of a shift. (2.1, 2.2)
I can graph equilibrium price and quantity and show surpluses and shortages. (2.6, 2.7)
I can predict the effect of single and double shifts on P and Q, including indeterminate cases. (2.7)
I can calculate PED with the midpoint method, classify demand, and identify the determinants of elasticity. (2.3)
I can predict and show graphically how a price change affects total revenue based on elasticity. (2.3)
I can calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity to classify goods. (2.4)
I can calculate PES and explain how time horizon affects responsiveness. (2.5)
I can apply elasticity to real markets with S&D graphs. (2.3–2.6)
I can graph a binding price ceiling or floor and identify the shortage or surplus. (2.8)
I can show the effect of a per-unit tax or subsidy on equilibrium P and Q. (2.8)
I can explain how elasticity determines whether buyers or sellers bear more of a tax. (2.8)

AP Microeconomics.learning_target_s:
CH 7 [CED 2.6, 1.6, 6.1]
EQ: How do we measure the benefit buyers and sellers get from a market, and why does a free market maximize it? (2.6, 6.1)
CH 10 [CED 6.1, 6.2]
EQ: When does a free market produce too much or too little of a good, and how can government or private bargaining fix it? (6.1, 6.2)
AP Microeconomics.success_criteria:
I can identify and calculate consumer surplus, producer surplus, and total surplus on a graph. (2.6)
I can explain why the competitive equilibrium is allocatively efficient (P = MC, MB = MC). (2.6, 6.1)
I can show how a price change changes consumer and producer surplus. (2.6)
I can graph a negative or positive externality using MSC/MPC and MSB/MPB and identify the market and socially optimal quantities. (6.2)
I can identify deadweight loss from an externality and show how a corrective (Pigouvian) tax or subsidy internalizes it. (6.1, 6.2)
I can explain the Coase theorem and the limits of private solutions. (6.2)

AP Microeconomics.unit: UNIT 4 — Taxes, Public Goods, and the Tax System
AP Microeconomics.learning_target_s:
CH 8 [CED 2.8]
EQ: Why does a tax cost society more than the revenue it raises, and what determines how much more? (2.8)
CH 11 [CED 6.3]
EQ: Why won't private markets provide lighthouses or protect fisheries, and what should government do about it? (6.3)
CH 12 [CED 6.5, 2.8]
EQ: What makes a tax system efficient and fair, and how do progressive, regressive, and proportional taxes differ? (6.5)
AP Microeconomics.success_criteria:
I can graph a per-unit tax and identify tax revenue, deadweight loss, and the change in consumer and producer surplus. (2.8)
I can explain how elasticity of supply and demand determines the size of deadweight loss and tax revenue. (2.8)
I can classify goods by rivalry and excludability (private, public, common resource, club/natural monopoly). (6.3)
I can explain the free-rider problem and the tragedy of the commons and evaluate policy responses. (6.3)
I can classify a tax as progressive, regressive, or proportional using average and marginal tax rates. (6.5)
I can explain the trade-off between tax efficiency (DWL, administrative burden) and equity (benefits principle, ability-to-pay). (6.5, 2.8)

AP Microeconomics.unit: UNIT 5 — Production, Cost, and Perfect Competition
AP Microeconomics.learning_target_s:
CH 13 [CED 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4]
EQ: How do a firm's costs behave as it produces more, in the short run and the long run? (3.1–3.3) • Why can a firm earn an accounting profit but an economic loss? (3.4)
CH 14 [CED 3.5, 3.6, 3.7]
EQ: How does a perfectly competitive firm decide how much to produce, whether to shut down, and whether to stay in the industry? (3.5–3.7) • Why do competitive firms earn zero economic profit in the long run? (3.7)
AP Microeconomics.success_criteria:
I can calculate marginal product and explain diminishing marginal returns. (3.1)
I can calculate and graph TC, FC, VC, AFC, AVC, ATC, and MC and explain why MC crosses AVC and ATC at their minimums. (3.2)
I can explain economies and diseconomies of scale using the LRATC curve. (3.3)
I can distinguish explicit from implicit costs and compute accounting vs. economic profit. (3.4)
I can describe perfect competition and explain why the firm is a price taker with P = MR = D = AR. (3.7)
I can find the profit-maximizing quantity (MR = MC) and identify profit or loss as an area on a graph. (3.5)
I can apply the shutdown rule (P < AVC) and explain entry/exit in the long run. (3.6)
I can draw side-by-side market and firm graphs and show the transition to long-run equilibrium (P = min ATC). (3.7)

AP Microeconomics.learning_target_s:
CH 15 [CED 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 6.4]
EQ: Why does a monopolist charge more and produce less than a competitive market, and what does society lose? (4.1, 4.2) • When and why do firms charge different customers different prices? (4.3)
CH 16 [CED 4.4]
EQ: How can a market have many firms and still not be perfectly competitive, and why is it inefficient in the long run? (4.4)
CH 17 [CED 4.5]
EQ: Why do a few large firms sometimes cooperate and sometimes compete, and how does game theory predict what they will do? (4.5)
AP Microeconomics.success_criteria:
I can explain sources of monopoly power and why MR < P for a price maker. (4.1, 4.2)
I can graph a monopoly, identify Q where MR = MC, price from demand, profit, and deadweight loss. (4.2)
I can graph and explain perfect price discrimination and its effect on output, surplus, and DWL. (4.3)
I can show the effects of price regulation (socially optimal vs. fair-return pricing) on a natural monopoly. (6.4)
I can graph monopolistic competition in short-run profit/loss and long-run zero-profit equilibrium. (4.4)
I can explain excess capacity and markup over MC, and evaluate advertising and brand names. (4.4)
I can describe oligopoly characteristics and interpret concentration ratios. (4.5)
I can read a payoff matrix, identify dominant strategies and Nash equilibrium, and explain the prisoners' dilemma. (4.5)
I can explain why cartels are unstable and how antitrust policy addresses collusion. (4.5, 6.4)

AP Microeconomics.unit: UNIT 7 — Factor Markets and Income Distribution
AP Microeconomics.learning_target_s:
CH 18 [CED 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4]
EQ: What determines how many workers a firm hires and what it pays them? (5.1–5.3) • How does a single dominant employer change the labor market outcome? (5.4)
CH 19 [CED 5.2, 5.4]
EQ: Why do some workers earn so much more than others? (5.2)
CH 20 [CED 6.5]
EQ: How do we measure inequality, and what are the trade-offs of policies that redistribute income? (6.5)
AP Microeconomics.success_criteria:
I can explain derived demand and calculate marginal revenue product and marginal factor cost. (5.1, 5.3)
I can identify shifts in factor demand and supply and their effect on wage and employment. (5.2)
I can apply the MRP = MFC hiring rule and the least-cost rule for combining inputs. (5.3)
I can graph a monopsony and compare its wage and employment to a competitive labor market. (5.4)
I can explain wage differentials using compensating differentials, human capital, ability, and signaling. (5.2)
I can evaluate the effect of a minimum wage or union in competitive and monopsonistic labor markets. (5.4)
I can interpret a Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient and describe how tax and transfer policy shifts them. (6.5)
I can explain sources of income inequality and evaluate redistribution policies for efficiency and equity trade-offs. (6.5)

AP Microeconomics.learning_target_s: EQ: How do the models of Units 1–6 fit together to explain how markets allocate resources — and when they fail? (CED 1–6)
AP Microeconomics.success_criteria:
I can complete a full-length AP-style multiple-choice set within the exam time limit. (1–6)
I can answer a long FRQ that combines a firm graph, a market graph, and a policy change. (3, 4, 6)
I can draw every required AP Micro graph (S&D, surplus, externality, cost curves, four market structures, factor market, Lorenz curve) correctly labeled from memory. (2–6)

AP Microeconomics.learning_target_s: EQ: What do I still need to master to earn a 5 on the AP Microeconomics exam? (CED 1–6)
AP Microeconomics.success_criteria:
I can identify my weakest CED topics from practice-exam data and close them before the exam. (1–6)
I can draw every required AP Micro graph correctly labeled from memory, in under 2 minutes each. (2–6)
I can complete the AP MC section (60 Q / 70 min) and FRQ section (1 long + 2 short / 60 min) at proficiency.

Keyboarding \u0026 Document Formatting.learning_target_s:
UNIT 1 — Getting Started  [ISBE 12005A001; NBEA Input Technologies]
Learning targets (essential questions):
• Why does posture, hand placement, and keeping eyes off the keys matter more than speed at the start?
• How do I register in KeyboardingOnline.com and document my own progress?
Success criteria:
◦ I can register, log in, and navigate KeyboardingOnline.com from the class page.
◦ I can demonstrate correct posture, wrist position, and home-row placement (index fingers on the bumps).
◦ I can key home-row and first reach keys by touch without looking at the keyboard.
◦ I can print/submit a lesson summary (Progress Report) for assessment.

UNIT 7 — Personal Business Letter Format  [ISBE 12005A001; NBEA Communication]
Learning targets (essential questions):
• How does a personal business letter differ from a memo in audience, tone, and format?
• Which of my documents best demonstrates my formatting skill, and why?
Success criteria:
◦ I can key a personal business letter (PBL 1–5) in block format with return address, date, inside address, salutation, body, and closing.
◦ I can apply correct spacing between letter parts and proofread for accuracy.
◦ I can select and submit my best memo (from CM 2–5) for a summative grade.

announcements.title: On Saturday, the EHS Cross Country team
announcements.text: hosted the 60 th Annual Edwardsville Cross Country Invitational. It was another successful weekend for the Girls, as they won the meet in dominating fashion by placing five runners in the top 8. Scoring for the Tigers were: 2nd: MacKenna Kerpan, 3rd: Morgan Popelar, 5th: Ella Thompson, 7th: Audrey Floyd and 8th: Heidi Stahlheber. Other medalist for the Tigers included: Willow Jackson, Zoe Scroggins, Ginny Siejka, Nova Shaw, Hannah Stahlheber, Emily Stahlheber, Cara Kielty, Ava Horsfall, Evelyn Bristow, Ainsley Goodwin, Katie Hall, Abigail Godard and Jillian Suhre. The boys also had a strong performance, finishing in 2 nd place. Will McGinnish led the Tigers with a 4 th place finish. Other medalist for the Tigers included: Jake Burris, Colin Luitjohan, Evan Davis, Preston Brown, Jack Whiteaker, Conner Osborne, Evan Thompson, Gage Gusewelle, Ryder Schickedanz, Harrison Jackstadt, and Colin Hanson. Congratulations on your outstanding performances!

announcements.title: Today’s Mindfulness Monday:
announcements.text: Mindfulness can happen during simple everyday moments. When you eat lunch today, take a moment to notice the taste, texture, and smell of your food instead of rushing through the meal. Slowing down for even a minute can help you feel more present and relaxed.
